Summary: The sources state that the speed of light in the International System of Units (SI) is defined as exactly 299,792,458 m/s. This definition was established to ensure that the metre is defined as the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This exact value was fixed by international agreement in 1983, and it is used to define the metre rather than the other way around.

### Relativity [...] ### Relativity

The speed of light in vacuum is constant, regardless of the motion of the source or the inertial reference frame of the observer.

### Speed

The speed of light in vacuum, c, forms the basis for the definition of the unit of speed, the metre per second.

The fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum, c, is defined exactly:

c \mspace{4mu} = 299 \mspace{4mu} 792 \mspace{4mu} 458 \ \text{m} \ \text{s}^{-1} [...] Inverting this relation gives an exact expression for the metre per second in terms of the speed of light in vacuum, c :

1 \mspace{4mu} \text{m} \mspace{4mu} \text{s}^{-1} \mspace{4mu} = \dfrac{1}{299 \mspace{4mu} 792 \mspace{4mu} 458} \mspace{4mu} c\\  

### Length or distance

The speed of light in vacuum, c, together with the hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium 133 atom, ΔνCs, forms the basis for the definition of the unit of length, the metre.

Summary: The CODATA speed of light defined value is exactly 299,792,458 m/s. Since 1983, the metre has been defined so that the speed of light in a vacuum is precisely this number. This fixed value is used to define the metre as the distance that light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The second is, in turn, defined by the length of time occupied by 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation emitted by a caesium-133 atom. This definition makes the speed of light a constant in the International System of Units (SI).
